MCSC-101.title: Asymptotic analysis and structures
MCSC-101.explanation: Big-O bounds growth from above; amortised analysis bounds an average over a worst-case sequence. Fibonacci heaps support efficient amortised decrease-key; splay trees move accessed nodes towards the root; dynamic trees represent changing forests.
MCSC-101.example: Repeated accesses to a splay tree can become cheaper as frequently used nodes move near the root.
MCSC-101.distinction: Worst-case cost concerns one operation; amortised cost applies to a sequence, without assuming random inputs.

MCSC-101.title: Network flows
MCSC-101.explanation: A feasible flow obeys edge capacities and conservation at intermediate vertices. The maximum-flow minimum-cut theorem equates maximum source-to-sink flow with the capacity of a smallest cut; minimum-cost flow also accounts for edge costs.
MCSC-101.example: For one source-to-sink path with capacities 3 and 2, at most 2 units can flow.
MCSC-101.distinction: Maximum flow optimises volume; minimum-cost flow optimises cost subject to required flow and capacities.

MCSC-101.title: Linear and semidefinite programming
MCSC-101.explanation: A linear programme optimises a linear objective under linear equalities and inequalities. Semidefinite programming generalises this using a positive semidefinite matrix constraint, useful for relaxations.
MCSC-101.example: Maximise 3x+2y subject to x+y≤4 and x,y≥0: allocating all 4 units to x gives objective 12.
MCSC-101.distinction: Integer constraints make a linear model discrete; its continuous relaxation can give a bound rather than a feasible integer solution.

MCSC-101.title: Approximation and intractability
MCSC-101.explanation: A polynomial-time approximation algorithm trades exact optimality for a proven quality guarantee on hard optimisation problems. The ratio is defined relative to an optimum and depends on whether the problem is minimisation or maximisation.
MCSC-101.example: A maximal matching gives a vertex cover with at most twice as many vertices as an optimal cover.
MCSC-101.distinction: An approximation guarantee is a proven bound; a heuristic may work well but need not offer one.

MCSC-101.title: Large data and randomisation
MCSC-101.explanation: Streaming algorithms use limited memory and often one pass. Compression represents data economically; compressed sensing recovers structured sparse signals under suitable measurement assumptions. Randomised algorithms use random choices with a stated success or runtime guarantee.
MCSC-101.example: Reservoir sampling maintains a uniform random sample from a stream of unknown length.
MCSC-101.distinction: Monte Carlo algorithms allow bounded error; Las Vegas algorithms are correct when they terminate but have random runtime.

MCSC-101.title: Geometry, parallelism and lab methods
MCSC-101.explanation: Computational geometry studies geometric objects and queries; parallel algorithms split work while accounting for synchronisation. The syllabus lab also includes search, sorting, linked lists, trees, BFS/DFS, spanning trees, string matching, greedy methods, dynamic programming and backtracking.
MCSC-101.example: Breadth-first search explores levels with a queue; depth-first search follows branches using a stack or recursion.
MCSC-101.distinction: Parallel speedup depends on serial work and communication, not simply the processor count.

MCSC-101.title: Residual graphs and augmenting paths
MCSC-101.explanation: A residual graph represents how much flow can still be sent or reversed on each edge. Ford–Fulkerson repeatedly finds an augmenting path and increases flow by its smallest residual capacity until no augmenting path remains.
MCSC-101.example: If a path has residual capacities 5, 2 and 4, its bottleneck is 2; augmenting by 2 saturates at least one edge.
MCSC-101.distinction: Reverse residual edges allow earlier choices to be revised; they are not necessarily original network edges.

MCSC-101.title: Complexity and reductions
MCSC-101.explanation: A decision problem asks a yes/no question. A polynomial-time reduction transforms one problem into another, showing that an efficient solution to the second would solve the first; NP-completeness combines membership in NP with NP-hardness.
MCSC-101.example: To show problem B is NP-hard, reduce a known NP-hard problem A to B and prove that yes-instances correspond.
MCSC-101.distinction: A reduction from A to B supports B being at least as hard as A; the direction matters.

MCSC-101.title: Dynamic programming and greedy strategies
MCSC-101.explanation: Dynamic programming stores solutions to overlapping subproblems and combines them using a recurrence. A greedy algorithm chooses a locally appealing step and needs a proof that those choices lead to an optimal result.
MCSC-101.example: For 0/1 knapsack, compare excluding an item with including it when capacity permits, using the preceding item row.
MCSC-101.distinction: A plausible greedy rule is not enough: 0/1 knapsack is not generally solved optimally by sorting items by value-to-weight ratio.

MCSC-104.title: Learning and validation
MCSC-104.explanation: Supervised learning estimates a mapping from labelled examples; unsupervised learning finds structure without target labels. Training fits parameters, validation selects a model, and a held-out test estimates final generalisation.
MCSC-104.example: In five-fold cross-validation, train on four folds and validate on the fifth, rotating until every fold has served as validation.
MCSC-104.distinction: Fit preprocessing only within each training fold to avoid leakage from validation data.

MCSC-104.title: Covariance, correlation and regression
MCSC-104.explanation: Covariance indicates joint variation; correlation standardises it. Linear regression predicts a continuous target as an intercept plus a weighted sum of features, often fitted by least squares.
MCSC-104.example: For y=2+3x, x=4 gives a prediction of 14; residuals are observed values minus predictions.
MCSC-104.distinction: Correlation measures linear association, not causation; multiple regression uses several predictors.

MCSC-104.title: Principal component analysis
MCSC-104.explanation: PCA centres data and identifies orthogonal directions of maximum variance using eigenvectors of a covariance matrix or singular value decomposition. Retaining a few components can reduce dimension.
MCSC-104.example: Highly correlated height and weight variables may largely vary along a single diagonal component.
MCSC-104.distinction: Feature selection retains original variables; PCA creates new combinations. Scale matters when units differ.

MCSC-104.title: Clustering
MCSC-104.explanation: Clustering groups similar examples using a distance or density criterion. k-means alternates assignments and centroid updates; hierarchical clustering builds nested groups; density methods identify dense regions and noise.
MCSC-104.example: With points near 1, 2 and 10, a two-centre solution may group 1 and 2 separately from 10.
MCSC-104.distinction: k-means requires a chosen k and favours compact groups; density-based methods can discover irregular shapes.

MCSC-104.title: Classification and feature selection
MCSC-104.explanation: A classifier predicts labels. k-nearest neighbours votes among nearby training examples; naive Bayes combines class priors and feature likelihoods under conditional independence; support vector machines seek a separating margin.
MCSC-104.example: A 3-nearest-neighbour classifier with labels A, A, B predicts A for a new point.
MCSC-104.distinction: Distance-based methods are sensitive to scaling; naive Bayes can work despite imperfect independence assumptions.

MCSC-104.title: Trees, ensembles and model quality
MCSC-104.explanation: Decision trees split features into regions; boosting sequentially combines weak learners. Bias describes systematic error while variance describes sensitivity to the training sample.
MCSC-104.example: A decision tree might split on attendance and then assignment score to predict a category.
MCSC-104.distinction: Cross-validation helps tune complexity, while a final untouched test set gives a less biased final assessment.

MCSC-104.title: Cross-validation and data leakage
MCSC-104.explanation: Cross-validation repeatedly fits and evaluates on different training and validation folds. Scaling, feature selection and imputation must be learned inside each training fold to avoid using validation information.
MCSC-104.example: In five-fold validation, fit a scaler on four folds, transform the held-out fold using those parameters, and repeat for each fold.
MCSC-104.distinction: A test set is reserved for final evaluation; repeatedly selecting models on it turns it into validation data.

MCSC-104.title: Naive Bayes and class imbalance
MCSC-104.explanation: Naive Bayes applies Bayes’ rule with a conditional-independence assumption between features given the class. For imbalanced data, report class-specific precision and recall rather than accuracy alone.
MCSC-104.example: If 100 cases contain 5 positives, predicting every case negative gives 95% accuracy but zero recall for the positive class.
MCSC-104.distinction: Precision asks how many predicted positives are correct; recall asks how many actual positives were found.

MCSC-104.title: Bias, variance and boosting
MCSC-104.explanation: A model with high bias may underfit, while a high-variance model can fit noise and change substantially across datasets. Boosting combines weak learners sequentially to improve a chosen objective.
MCSC-104.example: A shallow tree ensemble can correct patterns missed by earlier trees, but excessive fitting to noise can still hurt held-out performance.
MCSC-104.distinction: Bagging fits models largely in parallel on resampled data; boosting fits a sequence where later learners address earlier errors.

MCSC-201.title: IoT architecture and devices
MCSC-201.explanation: The Internet of Things connects sensing or actuating devices, networks, services and applications. A typical path runs from a sensor through a gateway to storage and a dashboard.
MCSC-201.example: A soil-moisture sensor sends readings to a gateway, which displays trends and can trigger irrigation.
MCSC-201.distinction: A microcontroller such as an Arduino-class board is typically resource constrained; a Raspberry Pi-class computer runs a fuller operating system.

MCSC-201.title: Networking and Linux
MCSC-201.explanation: IP addressing and subnetting group network interfaces; switches forward frames locally, routers connect networks, and access points provide wireless connectivity. Linux exposes network interfaces and device files to software.
MCSC-201.example: A gateway can bridge sensor traffic to a LAN while a router forwards traffic to a remote service.
MCSC-201.distinction: A hub repeats traffic; a switch forwards frames based on learned addresses. Device-file permissions affect access.

MCSC-201.title: Communication and protocols
MCSC-201.explanation: MQTT uses brokered publish–subscribe messaging; CoAP uses lightweight request–response messaging; HTTP supports widely used web APIs. 6LoWPAN adapts IPv6 packets to constrained low-power networks.
MCSC-201.example: A temperature sensor publishes to a broker topic and a dashboard subscribes to that topic.
MCSC-201.distinction: MQTT decouples publisher from subscriber; HTTP commonly uses direct client–server requests.

MCSC-201.title: Web services and data storage
MCSC-201.explanation: A server receives device messages, validates them and stores observations. Relational tables suit structured records and joins; document databases can hold flexible JSON-like records.
MCSC-201.example: A reading record can contain device ID, time, value and unit; a dashboard requests a time range.
MCSC-201.distinction: JSON is a data format; MySQL and MongoDB are databases with different data models.

MCSC-201.title: Security and privacy
MCSC-201.explanation: Identify devices, authenticate requests, encrypt suitable traffic, protect credentials and apply updates. Minimise collected data and design for failure, physical access and device lifecycle.
MCSC-201.example: A compromised sensor should not be able to issue administrator commands; assign it only the permissions it needs.
MCSC-201.distinction: Encryption protects confidentiality in transit, while authorisation controls permitted actions.

MCSC-201.title: Applications and laboratory
MCSC-201.explanation: IoT supports monitoring, remote control, industrial systems, agriculture and healthcare. Evaluate accuracy, latency, availability, energy and safety for the use case.
MCSC-201.example: A greenhouse sensor samples periodically; compare measured temperature against a calibrated reference before automating control.
MCSC-201.distinction: Monitoring observes conditions; closed-loop control acts and observes the result. Validate sensor calibration and failure behaviour.

MCSC-201.title: Addressing, subnetting and routing
MCSC-201.explanation: An IPv4 subnet mask identifies the network prefix and host portion. A router forwards packets between networks using routes; a switch forwards Ethernet frames within a local network.
MCSC-201.example: A /24 IPv4 prefix contains 256 addresses in total; usable host-address conventions depend on the subnet and network context.
MCSC-201.distinction: A MAC address identifies a link-layer interface on a local link; an IP address supports network-layer addressing and routing.

MCSC-201.title: MQTT quality of service and device lifecycle
MCSC-201.explanation: MQTT connects clients through a broker and offers delivery levels: QoS 0 at most once, QoS 1 at least once, and QoS 2 exactly once at the MQTT protocol level.
MCSC-201.example: A sensor using QoS 1 may cause a duplicate message after retransmission, so an application should handle duplicates appropriately.
MCSC-201.distinction: A protocol delivery guarantee does not ensure a physical sensor reading is accurate or an actuator performed an action.

MCSC-201.title: IoT data quality and resilience
MCSC-201.explanation: Sensor systems must consider calibration, timestamps, missing readings, power loss, connectivity interruptions and safe update procedures. Analyse end-to-end delay rather than network latency alone.
MCSC-201.example: A gateway can timestamp readings, buffer a bounded number while offline and transmit them after reconnecting, while preserving their original observation times.
MCSC-201.distinction: A measurement may be unavailable, stale or invalid; these states should not silently become zero.

MMLC-201.title: Artificial neurons and network architectures
MMLC-201.explanation: An artificial neuron computes a weighted sum plus bias and applies an activation. Feed-forward networks pass information forward; recurrent networks also use state from earlier steps.
MMLC-201.example: For weights 0.5 and 1, inputs 2 and 1, and bias 0, the pre-activation is 2.
MMLC-201.distinction: Biological neurons inspire the abstraction, but an artificial neuron is a simplified mathematical model.

MMLC-201.title: Training and backpropagation
MMLC-201.explanation: A loss measures prediction error. Backpropagation applies the chain rule to compute gradients; an optimiser adjusts weights to reduce loss on training data.
MMLC-201.example: With loss (w−3)² at w=1, its gradient is −4. A small gradient-descent step increases w towards 3.
MMLC-201.distinction: Training error measures fitted data; validation error helps reveal poor generalisation.

MMLC-201.title: Fuzzy sets and membership
MMLC-201.explanation: A fuzzy set assigns membership in [0,1], expressing degree of membership in a specified set. Membership functions can be triangular, trapezoidal or other shapes.
MMLC-201.example: A temperature of 28°C might have membership 0.6 in the set warm, depending on the chosen function.
MMLC-201.distinction: Fuzzy membership expresses graded belonging; probability represents uncertainty about an event.

MMLC-201.title: Fuzzy inference and control
MMLC-201.explanation: Rules combine fuzzy premises and conclusions, such as IF temperature is high THEN fan speed is fast. Fuzzification maps inputs to memberships; inference combines rules; defuzzification produces a crisp output.
MMLC-201.example: A controller can combine warm and hot memberships to produce an intermediate fan setting.
MMLC-201.distinction: A fuzzy rule system represents expert rules; a neural network learns parameters from data.

MMLC-201.title: Genetic algorithms
MMLC-201.explanation: Genetic algorithms evolve candidate solutions using selection, crossover and mutation, guided by a fitness function. Encoding determines how a candidate is represented.
MMLC-201.example: A bit string can encode a subset of features; selection favours candidates with good validation fitness and mutation flips occasional bits.
MMLC-201.distinction: Crossover recombines parents; mutation introduces variation. Neither guarantees a global optimum.

MMLC-201.title: Deep models and regularisation
MMLC-201.explanation: Deep feed-forward networks, CNNs, RNNs and deep belief networks learn different representations. Dropout and other regularisers can reduce overfitting; model selection requires separate validation.
MMLC-201.example: A CNN shares filters over an image, while an RNN processes a sequence with a recurring hidden state.
MMLC-201.distinction: Dropout is a training technique, whereas a CNN is an architectural family.

MMLC-201.title: Perceptron and linear separability
MMLC-201.explanation: A perceptron applies a threshold to a weighted sum. The perceptron learning rule adjusts weights after a misclassification; a single-layer linear decision boundary cannot represent every Boolean function.
MMLC-201.example: The AND function is linearly separable, but XOR is not separable by one straight line in its two-dimensional binary input space.
MMLC-201.distinction: A multilayer network with nonlinear hidden units can represent functions that a single linear threshold unit cannot.

MMLC-201.title: Fuzzy membership and defuzzification
MMLC-201.explanation: A membership function maps an input to a degree from 0 to 1. Fuzzy inference combines rule activations and an output membership shape; defuzzification converts that result to a crisp action.
MMLC-201.example: A triangular membership function with vertices (20,0), (25,1), (30,0) gives membership 0.6 at 27.
MMLC-201.distinction: A fuzzy membership of 0.6 is a degree of belonging to a chosen set, not necessarily a 60% probability.

MMLC-201.title: Genetic representation and selection
MMLC-201.explanation: A genetic algorithm encodes each candidate, evaluates fitness, selects parents, applies crossover and mutation, and iterates. Representation, fitness and constraints determine what solutions are searchable.
MMLC-201.example: To select three features from a set of ten, use a ten-bit string and penalise or repair candidates that do not contain exactly three ones.
MMLC-201.distinction: Mutation introduces variation; selection changes which candidates contribute to later generations.

MCSE-202.title: Data, samples and bias
MCSE-202.explanation: Data science frames a question, collects data, analyses it and communicates conclusions. A population includes all units of interest; a sample is the subset observed. Selection and measurement bias can distort conclusions.
MCSE-202.example: An online survey about internet use excludes people without access, so its sample may not represent the whole population.
MCSE-202.distinction: Random sampling addresses selection mechanisms; a large but biased sample is not automatically representative.

MCSE-202.title: Summary statistics and exploratory analysis
MCSE-202.explanation: Mean, median, spread and quantiles describe distributions. Histograms, scatter plots and box plots reveal shape, outliers and relationships before modelling.
MCSE-202.example: For 1, 2, 3, 4, 100, the mean is 22 but the median is 3, illustrating sensitivity to an outlier.
MCSE-202.distinction: A histogram shows a distribution; a scatter plot shows pairs of numerical values.

MCSE-202.title: Probability and inference
MCSE-202.explanation: Conditional probability describes an event given evidence. Bayes’ rule combines a prior with a likelihood; intervals and hypothesis tests quantify uncertainty under assumptions.
MCSE-202.example: If P(A)=0.5, P(B|A)=0.8 and P(B)=0.5, Bayes’ rule gives P(A|B)=0.8.
MCSE-202.distinction: A confidence interval is a procedure with long-run coverage, not automatically a posterior probability about a fixed parameter.

MCSE-202.title: Association, confounding and Simpson’s paradox
MCSE-202.explanation: Association does not by itself establish causation. A confounder affects both an exposure and an outcome; Simpson’s paradox occurs when an aggregate trend reverses or changes across groups.
MCSE-202.example: Treatment success can appear lower overall if the treated group contains more severe cases, despite higher success within each severity group.
MCSE-202.distinction: Stratification can reveal group differences; causal conclusions still need a justified design and assumptions.

MCSE-202.title: Regression and predictive models
MCSE-202.explanation: Linear regression predicts a numeric outcome. k-nearest neighbours predicts from nearby examples; naive Bayes estimates class probabilities; k-means groups unlabelled data.
MCSE-202.example: A model can estimate house price from area and location, but it must be evaluated on homes not used for fitting.
MCSE-202.distinction: k-nearest neighbours is supervised when trained with labels; k-means is an unsupervised clustering method.

MCSE-202.title: Bayesian modelling and communication
MCSE-202.explanation: Bayesian inference updates a prior distribution using data likelihood to obtain a posterior. Hierarchical models share information across groups while allowing group-level differences.
MCSE-202.example: A prior for each district’s rate can be linked to a common population distribution, then updated with district observations.
MCSE-202.distinction: Posterior uncertainty depends on the model and prior; diagnostic plots and clear uncertainty reporting remain essential.

MCSE-202.title: Simpson’s paradox and group composition
MCSE-202.explanation: An association in aggregate data can reverse after dividing data into relevant groups, because the group mix differs. Inspect denominators and group-level rates before interpreting a summary.
MCSE-202.example: Treatment A succeeds in 9/10 easy and 50/100 hard cases, while B succeeds in 80/100 easy and 4/10 hard cases. A has a higher success rate in each group, but A is 59/110 overall and B is 84/110 because their group composition differs.
MCSE-202.distinction: A reversal signals that aggregation matters; it does not by itself identify a causal effect.

MCSE-202.title: Leakage and validation pipelines
MCSE-202.explanation: Leakage occurs when information unavailable at prediction time influences training or model selection. Fit preprocessing only on training partitions and keep a final test set separate.
MCSE-202.example: If the mean used for imputation is calculated using all records before a train–test split, test-set information has entered training.
MCSE-202.distinction: A random split can be misleading for temporal data; a chronological split may better match the deployment scenario.

MCSE-202.title: Bayesian updating and prior choice
MCSE-202.explanation: Bayesian inference combines a prior distribution with a likelihood to produce a posterior. A posterior predictive distribution incorporates uncertainty about model parameters in predictions.
MCSE-202.example: With a Beta(1,1) prior and 8 successes in 10 independent Bernoulli observations, the posterior is Beta(9,3).
MCSE-202.distinction: A posterior depends on the likelihood and prior; sensitivity checks can reveal when conclusions depend strongly on assumptions.

MMLE-201.title: Big data and distributed systems
MMLE-201.explanation: Big data problems arise when volume, velocity, variety or processing needs exceed convenient single-machine approaches. Distributed systems split storage and computation across machines.
MMLE-201.example: A stream of device events can be partitioned and processed by multiple workers.
MMLE-201.distinction: More data is not automatically better: quality, governance, cost and bias still matter.

MMLE-201.title: Hadoop and HDFS
MMLE-201.explanation: Hadoop provides a distributed ecosystem; HDFS stores large files in blocks across machines and supports fault tolerance through replication. The NameNode manages metadata and DataNodes store blocks.
MMLE-201.example: A large file can be divided into blocks stored across several nodes; replicas help tolerate node failure.
MMLE-201.distinction: HDFS is designed for large-scale throughput; it is not a direct replacement for low-latency transactional storage.

MMLE-201.title: MapReduce and data movement
MMLE-201.explanation: MapReduce applies a map operation to input records, groups intermediate values by key, and reduces each group. Input ingestion and output retrieval form part of a complete pipeline.
MMLE-201.example: Word count emits (word,1) pairs in map and sums values for each word in reduce.
MMLE-201.distinction: Map transforms individual records; reduce aggregates values sharing a key.

MMLE-201.title: Hive and HiveQL
MMLE-201.explanation: Hive provides a SQL-like interface for querying data stored in a Hadoop environment. Tables describe schemas and queries are translated into execution plans.
MMLE-201.example: A HiveQL query can group event records by day and count rows per group.
MMLE-201.distinction: HiveQL resembles SQL but its execution and transaction features depend on the configured engine and storage.

MMLE-201.title: Pig and HBase
MMLE-201.explanation: Pig provides a data-flow language for transformations; HBase is a distributed, column-family-oriented database built for different access patterns than batch queries.
MMLE-201.example: A batch pipeline can transform logs before a serving system retrieves records by key.
MMLE-201.distinction: Hive is commonly used for analytic queries; HBase targets keyed access over large distributed tables.

MMLE-201.title: Spark and machine learning
MMLE-201.explanation: Spark processes distributed data with reusable computations and supports machine-learning workflows through Spark ML. H2O and Azure ML provide alternative tools or platforms named in the syllabus.
MMLE-201.example: Split data before fitting transformations, train a classifier and evaluate it on held-out records.
MMLE-201.distinction: Distributed training addresses scale, but does not by itself solve leakage, bias or poor evaluation.

MMLE-201.title: HDFS blocks and fault tolerance
MMLE-201.explanation: HDFS separates file-system metadata from data blocks. A configured replication factor creates copies on different nodes, and the system attempts recovery when a copy becomes unavailable.
MMLE-201.example: If the replication factor is 3, the system targets three replicas of each block subject to cluster conditions and placement policy.
MMLE-201.distinction: Replication improves availability but is not a substitute for an independent backup or protection from logical deletion.

MMLE-201.title: MapReduce word-count trace
MMLE-201.explanation: A mapper emits intermediate key–value pairs; the shuffle groups values by key; reducers aggregate each group. This separation allows work to be distributed.
MMLE-201.example: For “cat dog cat”, map emits (cat,1), (dog,1), (cat,1); shuffle groups cat:[1,1], dog:[1]; reduce emits cat:2 and dog:1.
MMLE-201.distinction: MapReduce is a programming model; Hadoop is an ecosystem that includes an implementation and storage components.

MMLE-201.title: Hive partitions and query design
MMLE-201.explanation: Partitioning organises data by selected fields so a query can skip irrelevant partitions when filtering. Tables may be managed or external depending on configuration and engine version.
MMLE-201.example: Partitioning event data by date can avoid reading other dates for a date-filtered query.
MMLE-201.distinction: Partitioning can improve targeted scans, but too many tiny partitions or files can add overhead.

MMLC-301.title: Probability, likelihood and loss
MMLC-301.explanation: Deep learning fits models with multiple learned transformations. Maximum likelihood chooses parameters that make observed data likely under a model; losses often express the negative log-likelihood.
MMLC-301.example: For binary classification, cross-entropy penalises a confidently wrong predicted probability heavily.
MMLC-301.distinction: Mean squared error is common for numerical predictions; cross-entropy is commonly used with class probabilities.

MMLC-301.title: Feed-forward networks and activations
MMLC-301.explanation: An MLP applies affine transformations and nonlinear activations through hidden layers. Sigmoid and tanh are bounded; ReLU is max(0,z); softmax turns logits into probabilities across classes.
MMLC-301.example: For logits (0,0), softmax assigns probability 0.5 to each class.
MMLC-301.distinction: Without nonlinearities, a composition of linear layers is still a linear transformation.

MMLC-301.title: Backpropagation and gradient descent
MMLC-301.explanation: The chain rule propagates derivatives from loss to each layer. Gradient descent updates a parameter θ as θ ← θ − η∇L; the learning rate η affects training.
MMLC-301.example: For L=(θ−3)² and θ=1, the gradient is −4; with η=0.1, the next θ is 1.4.
MMLC-301.distinction: Backpropagation computes gradients; the optimiser decides how parameters are updated.

MMLC-301.title: Generalisation and training
MMLC-301.explanation: Overfitting occurs when training performance is much better than performance on new data. Regularisation, dropout, suitable augmentation and early stopping can help; GPUs speed suitable parallel computations.
MMLC-301.example: Monitor validation loss after each epoch and keep the checkpoint selected by a predeclared validation rule.
MMLC-301.distinction: A GPU changes execution speed, not the validity of an evaluation. Tune on validation data, not the test set.

MMLC-301.title: CNNs and sequence models
MMLC-301.explanation: CNNs apply shared filters to local regions, often combining convolution, activation and pooling. RNNs carry hidden state across a sequence; both require task-appropriate data and evaluation.
MMLC-301.example: A CNN can learn image patterns; an RNN can process a sequence of sensor measurements.
MMLC-301.distinction: CNN weight sharing exploits spatial locality; recurrent connections encode sequential context.

MMLC-301.title: Transfer and generative models
MMLC-301.explanation: Transfer learning reuses representations learned on one task for another. Autoencoders reconstruct input through a bottleneck; generative models learn a model of data, while deep belief networks combine layers of probabilistic representations.
MMLC-301.example: A pretrained image encoder can be fine-tuned for a smaller labelled dataset after checking that training and evaluation data do not overlap.
MMLC-301.distinction: An autoencoder’s reconstruction objective differs from a classifier’s label-prediction objective.

MMLC-301.title: Convolution dimensions and receptive fields
MMLC-301.explanation: A convolutional layer uses a kernel applied across an input. For one dimension, output size is floor((n+2p−k)/s)+1 for input n, padding p, kernel k and stride s, assuming unit dilation.
MMLC-301.example: For n=32, k=3, p=1 and s=1, the output size is 32. With the same settings and s=2, it is 16.
MMLC-301.distinction: A feature map is the result of applying learned filters; a receptive field describes which input positions can affect an output.

MMLC-301.title: Regularisation and evaluation
MMLC-301.explanation: Regularisation limits effective model complexity or discourages overfitting. Weight decay, dropout and early stopping affect training differently; compare them using a validation protocol.
MMLC-301.example: If training loss falls while validation loss rises over several epochs, evaluate whether the model is overfitting before selecting a checkpoint.
MMLC-301.distinction: Dropout changes activations during training; weight decay penalises or shrinks parameters, depending on the optimiser’s implementation.

MMLC-301.title: Transfer learning and data leakage
MMLC-301.explanation: Transfer learning adapts parameters learned on a source task to a target task, often by training a new head and optionally fine-tuning earlier layers. Check dataset overlap and distribution mismatch.
MMLC-301.example: A pretrained image encoder can be evaluated on a new task with the test set kept separate from fine-tuning and model selection.
MMLC-301.distinction: Feature extraction freezes the encoder; fine-tuning updates some or all pretrained parameters.

MMLE-302.title: Agent, environment and return
MMLE-302.explanation: In reinforcement learning an agent observes a state, chooses an action, receives a reward and moves to a next state. A policy maps states to actions or action probabilities; return sums future rewards, often with discount γ.
MMLE-302.example: A robot receives −1 per step and +10 at a goal. With γ=0.9, a reward one step later contributes 9 to present return.
MMLE-302.distinction: Reward is an immediate signal; return summarises a trajectory’s future rewards.

MMLE-302.title: Markov processes and value functions
MMLE-302.explanation: The Markov property means the current state contains the relevant information needed to predict the next transition given an action. A value function estimates expected return from a state under a policy.
MMLE-302.example: For a terminal action paying 5, with no later reward, its return is 5.
MMLE-302.distinction: A state-value function V(s) evaluates a state; an action-value function Q(s,a) evaluates a state–action pair.

MMLE-302.title: Planning with a known model
MMLE-302.explanation: A transition model gives probabilities and rewards for actions. Policy iteration alternates evaluating and improving a policy; value iteration repeatedly applies a Bellman optimality backup.
MMLE-302.example: In a small grid with known transition probabilities, compare the expected discounted return of available moves.
MMLE-302.distinction: Policy iteration evaluates an explicit policy; value iteration applies a greedy optimality update directly.

MMLE-302.title: Model-free control
MMLE-302.explanation: When transition probabilities are unknown, temporal-difference methods learn from observed transitions. Q-learning uses the maximum estimated next-action value; SARSA uses the next action actually chosen by its policy.
MMLE-302.example: Q-learning updates Q(s,a) towards r+γ maxₐ′ Q(s′,a′); SARSA instead uses Q(s′,a′) for the selected next action.
MMLE-302.distinction: Q-learning is off-policy; SARSA is on-policy. Both require suitable learning conditions for classical tabular guarantees.

MMLE-302.title: Exploration and approximation
MMLE-302.explanation: An agent must gather information as well as use its current estimates. ε-greedy chooses a random action with probability ε and otherwise acts greedily; function approximation generalises across large state spaces.
MMLE-302.example: With ε=0.1, a random action is selected on 10% of decisions, subject to the chosen random-action distribution.
MMLE-302.distinction: Exploration can discover better actions but may be unsafe; safety and evaluation must be considered separately.

MMLE-302.title: Imitation, offline and search
MMLE-302.explanation: Imitation learning learns behaviour from demonstrations; offline RL learns from a fixed dataset and must handle actions poorly represented in that data. Monte Carlo tree search builds a search tree using sampled rollouts; meta-learning studies adaptation across tasks.
MMLE-302.example: A game-playing agent can use simulated rollouts to compare candidate moves before acting.
MMLE-302.distinction: Offline evaluation is difficult when the target policy differs greatly from the data-collection policy.

MMLE-302.title: Bellman expectation and optimality
MMLE-302.explanation: The Bellman expectation equation expresses a policy’s value as expected immediate reward plus discounted value of the next state. The optimality equation chooses the best action at each state.
MMLE-302.example: If a state has a certain reward 2 and leads to a state valued at 5 with γ=0.9, its one-step backed-up value is 6.5.
MMLE-302.distinction: Policy evaluation follows a fixed policy; optimality backups compare available actions.

MMLE-302.title: Q-learning and SARSA updates
MMLE-302.explanation: Both use sampled transitions, a learning rate and a temporal-difference target. Q-learning uses the largest next action value; SARSA uses the value of the next action selected by the behaviour policy.
MMLE-302.example: If old Q=2, α=0.5, r=1, γ=0.9 and the maximum next Q=4, a Q-learning update yields 3.3.
MMLE-302.distinction: Q-learning is off-policy because its target is greedy even when behaviour explores; SARSA’s target follows the behaviour action.

MMLE-302.title: Offline reinforcement learning and evaluation
MMLE-302.explanation: Offline RL uses a fixed dataset rather than collecting new interaction while learning. The learned policy can choose actions rarely represented in the data, making value estimates unreliable.
MMLE-302.example: A policy trained from historical control logs should be checked for actions outside the logging policy’s coverage before any live use.
MMLE-302.distinction: Imitation learning copies behaviour from demonstrations; offline RL uses rewards and transitions to optimise a policy from a fixed dataset.

MCSC-106.title: Defining an independent study
MCSC-106.explanation: Start with a manageable topic and formulate a question whose scope can be investigated with the time and resources available. Agree goals and milestones with a supervisor.
MCSC-106.example: Replace “study AI security” with a focused question about one clearly defined threat and setting.
MCSC-106.distinction: A topic names an area; a research question states what you intend to investigate.

MCSC-106.title: Finding and assessing sources
MCSC-106.explanation: Search scholarly databases, trace references and evaluate relevance, methods, limitations and publication context. Keep a record of search terms and decisions.
MCSC-106.example: Create a literature matrix listing problem, data, method, result and limitation for each paper.
MCSC-106.distinction: A literature review synthesises and compares sources rather than merely listing abstracts.

MCSC-106.title: Research integrity and progress
MCSC-106.explanation: Record methods and sources, cite borrowed work, retain reproducible notes and report uncertainty. Confirm progress and submission requirements with your supervisor.
MCSC-106.example: Maintain a dated log of experiments, code versions, observations and next steps.
MCSC-106.distinction: A preliminary result is evidence to examine, not a conclusion that must be defended regardless of contrary data.

MCSC-106.title: Search strategies and evidence tables
MCSC-106.explanation: Build a search using concept blocks joined with AND and synonyms joined with OR. Record databases, dates, exact queries and selection criteria so the search can be revisited.
MCSC-106.example: A query might combine (phishing OR fraudulent website) with (detection OR classification); screen title and abstract against a defined question.
MCSC-106.distinction: A systematic search follows a documented process; a narrative overview may be broader and less reproducible.

MCSC-106.title: Research questions and operational definitions
MCSC-106.explanation: A useful question defines the setting, variables and intended comparison. An operational definition states how an abstract construct will be observed or measured.
MCSC-106.example: Define detection latency as elapsed time between an event arriving and a decision being produced, measured by a specified clock and protocol.
MCSC-106.distinction: A conceptual definition explains meaning; an operational definition explains measurement.

MCSC-202.title: Developing the research plan
MCSC-202.explanation: Refine a research question, review prior work and justify a method appropriate to the question. Define measurable outcomes and a feasible timetable with your supervisor.
MCSC-202.example: For a classification study, specify the dataset, baseline, split, metrics and intended analysis before training.
MCSC-202.distinction: A research objective states the aim; a method explains how evidence will be gathered.

MCSC-202.title: Pilot and evaluation
MCSC-202.explanation: A pilot checks feasibility and can expose data, measurement or implementation problems before a full study. Document changes rather than treating exploratory decisions as preplanned.
MCSC-202.example: Run a small pipeline end to end to detect missing labels and estimate processing time.
MCSC-202.distinction: A pilot checks the process; a final evaluation supports the study’s conclusions.

MCSC-202.title: Ethics and reproducibility
MCSC-202.explanation: Consider consent, privacy, data rights, security and the limitations of any available sample. Record versions and assumptions so results can be checked.
MCSC-202.example: Store only needed data and explain any permissions or approval required by the institution.
MCSC-202.distinction: Reproducibility of a computation does not by itself establish that its data or conclusions are valid.

MCSC-202.title: Research designs and baselines
MCSC-202.explanation: Choose an observational, experimental, simulation or other design according to the question, available resources and ethical constraints. Define a baseline that makes the proposed contribution meaningful.
MCSC-202.example: A system comparison can use the same dataset and evaluation split for both a proposed model and a simple existing baseline.
MCSC-202.distinction: A baseline is a reference for comparison; a control condition is defined by an experimental design.

MCSC-202.title: Pilot studies and protocol changes
MCSC-202.explanation: A pilot checks whether recruitment, instruments, data handling or code are workable. Record changes made after the pilot and distinguish planned from exploratory analysis.
MCSC-202.example: A pilot of ten sample records may reveal malformed timestamps before the full data pipeline is run.
MCSC-202.distinction: A successful pilot does not guarantee adequate statistical power or unbiased results in the full study.

MCSC-302.title: Dissertation I: proposal and literature
MCSC-302.explanation: Define a focused research problem, review the literature and show the gap your proposed work addresses. Agree the scope and institutional milestones with your supervisor.
MCSC-302.example: A proposal can state the problem, motivation, research questions, method, resources and expected evaluation.
MCSC-302.distinction: A research gap is an evidence-backed limitation in prior work, not simply an area with many publications.

MCSC-302.title: Method and feasibility
MCSC-302.explanation: Select data, baselines, metrics and an analysis plan suited to the question; check practical, ethical and access constraints. Use a pilot to assess feasibility.
MCSC-302.example: Before an experiment, define a train–validation–test separation and a baseline appropriate to the task.
MCSC-302.distinction: A feasibility result supports a plan; it is not necessarily the final study result.

MCSC-302.title: Documenting progress
MCSC-302.explanation: Maintain versioned code and data references, document assumptions and report deviations from the plan. Departmental rules determine the precise submission and review process.
MCSC-302.example: Keep a research log and a short progress report describing work completed, evidence, issues and next steps.
MCSC-302.distinction: A milestone is a planning aid; formal assessment requirements come from your institution.

MCSC-302.title: Literature synthesis and research gap
MCSC-302.explanation: Compare previous studies by problem, dataset, method, evaluation and limitations. Define a gap that follows from that comparison and a question that can be addressed with available evidence.
MCSC-302.example: If published models are tested only on one dataset, a proposed study might evaluate generalisation across clearly identified datasets, subject to access and comparability.
MCSC-302.distinction: A topic is a broad area; a gap is a specific supported limitation or unresolved question.

MCSC-302.title: Methodology and study protocol
MCSC-302.explanation: Specify data provenance, inclusion rules, preprocessing, baselines, outcome measures, analysis and ethical safeguards before conducting the study where feasible.
MCSC-302.example: A classification protocol can define dataset versions, leakage-resistant splits, baseline models, metrics and a plan for handling failures.
MCSC-302.distinction: A pilot checks whether a procedure works; it does not guarantee that the full study is unbiased or adequately powered.

MCSC-401.title: Dissertation II: execution and analysis
MCSC-401.explanation: Carry out the agreed study, record procedures and analyse results against the research questions. Clearly separate planned analyses from exploratory findings.
MCSC-401.example: Compare a proposed method with specified baselines on the same evaluation protocol and report uncertainty where appropriate.
MCSC-401.distinction: A measured improvement is not automatically evidence of causation or real-world usefulness.

MCSC-401.title: Writing and presentation
MCSC-401.explanation: A dissertation commonly presents the problem, related work, methods, results, discussion, limitations and references. Follow your department’s current formatting and submission requirements.
MCSC-401.example: A results section reports observations; a discussion interprets their meaning and limitations.
MCSC-401.distinction: Results describe what was observed; discussion explains implications without overstating them.

MCSC-401.title: Reproducibility and final checks
MCSC-401.explanation: Verify citations, figure permissions, data handling, calculations and reproducibility. Document what can and cannot be shared and secure any necessary approvals.
MCSC-401.example: Record software versions, dataset provenance, configuration and steps needed to rerun an analysis.
MCSC-401.distinction: Reproducible code supports checking, but valid design and representative data remain separate requirements.

MCSC-102.title: Conditional probability and Bayes’ rule
MCSC-102.explanation: Conditional probability updates an event probability when another event is known: P(A|B)=P(A∩B)/P(B), for P(B)>0. Bayes’ rule reverses the conditioning using a prior and likelihood.
MCSC-102.example: If P(A)=0.2, P(B|A)=0.8 and P(B|not A)=0.1, then P(B)=0.24 and P(A|B)=2/3.
MCSC-102.distinction: Mutually exclusive events cannot occur together; independent events satisfy P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B).

MCSC-102.title: Estimation, confidence intervals and tests
MCSC-102.explanation: A point estimate summarises a parameter with one value; a confidence interval is produced by a procedure designed to cover the fixed parameter at a stated long-run rate under assumptions. Hypothesis testing evaluates data against a null model.
MCSC-102.example: A 95% confidence-interval method would cover the true parameter in about 95% of repeated samples under its assumptions.
MCSC-102.distinction: A p-value is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true. Sampling bias is not cured by a larger sample alone.

MCSC-102.title: Markov chains and queues
MCSC-102.explanation: A Markov chain models transitions between states where the present state supplies the information relevant to the next transition. Queueing models use arrival and service processes to study waiting and congestion.
MCSC-102.example: For transitions P(0→1)=0.2 and P(0→0)=0.8, a system currently in state 0 moves to state 1 next step with probability 0.2.
MCSC-102.distinction: A stationary distribution describes a long-run state distribution when applicable; it is not the same as a single transition probability.

MCSC-103.title: Layered communication and encapsulation
MCSC-103.explanation: Layering assigns communication responsibilities to protocols. Application data is carried by transport, network and link mechanisms; encapsulation adds control information at each relevant layer.
MCSC-103.example: A web request may use HTTP over TCP, IP and a local Ethernet or Wi-Fi link. A receiver processes the layers in reverse.
MCSC-103.distinction: A protocol specifies rules between peers; a layer is a way to organise responsibilities.

MCSC-103.title: Error detection, retransmission and recovery
MCSC-103.explanation: A checksum or cyclic redundancy check detects many transmission errors; error-correcting codes add redundancy that can permit correction. Retransmission protocols can recover lost data when the communication design allows feedback.
MCSC-103.example: With a simple parity bit, adding one parity bit can detect an odd number of bit flips, but cannot reliably detect every multi-bit error.
MCSC-103.distinction: Detection identifies an invalid received pattern; correction reconstructs data only under the code’s guarantees.

MCSC-103.title: SNMP, management and security
MCSC-103.explanation: SNMP management stations query or receive notifications about managed devices through management information represented by objects. Configuration, fault and performance management address different operational needs.
MCSC-103.example: A manager can monitor interface counters to identify increasing packet drops and investigate a fault.
MCSC-103.distinction: Monitoring identifies conditions; access control, authentication and encryption address different security requirements. SNMP versions have different security properties.

MCSC-105.title: Proof techniques and recurrence relations
MCSC-105.explanation: Mathematical induction proves a base case and then proves that a statement at one index implies the next. A recurrence defines later values using earlier values and initial conditions.
MCSC-105.example: If aₙ=2aₙ₋₁ and a₀=1, repeated substitution gives aₙ=2ⁿ.
MCSC-105.distinction: A recurrence states how terms depend on previous terms; a closed form gives an expression directly in n.

MCSC-105.title: Trees, connectivity and spanning structures
MCSC-105.explanation: A connected undirected graph has a path between every pair of vertices. A tree is a connected acyclic undirected graph; a spanning tree connects all vertices without a cycle.
MCSC-105.example: A connected graph with four vertices has a spanning tree with three edges; different spanning trees can have different total weights.
MCSC-105.distinction: A minimum spanning tree minimises total tree-edge weight; a shortest-path tree minimises distances from one chosen source.

MCSC-105.title: Matching and network applications
MCSC-105.explanation: A matching is a set of edges that share no endpoint. Bipartite matching can model assignments between two sets, while network flows represent movement subject to capacities.
MCSC-105.example: Students and projects form two vertex sets; a matching assigns a project to a student without assigning either twice.
MCSC-105.distinction: Maximum-cardinality matching maximises the number of matched edges; weighted assignment can optimise a separate cost or benefit.

MMLC-202.title: Decision boundaries and generalisation
MMLC-202.explanation: A classifier divides a feature space into regions that lead to predicted labels. Its decision boundary depends on the representation, learned parameters and training data.
MMLC-202.example: A linear classifier in two dimensions divides the plane with a line; a nonlinear model can represent more complex boundaries.
MMLC-202.distinction: A training decision boundary may fit the observed samples well while failing on new samples.

MMLC-202.title: Feature selection and dimensionality reduction
MMLC-202.explanation: Feature selection chooses a subset of original variables. Dimensionality reduction creates a lower-dimensional representation; PCA is an unsupervised linear method that prioritises variance.
MMLC-202.example: If measurements are highly correlated, PCA may summarise much of their variation in fewer components, after appropriate scaling.
MMLC-202.distinction: High variance does not necessarily mean high class-discrimination value; evaluate the representation for the task.

MMLC-202.title: Precision, recall and error trade-offs
MMLC-202.explanation: Precision is TP/(TP+FP), while recall is TP/(TP+FN), when the denominators are nonzero. The decision threshold and class prevalence influence the practical meaning of results.
MMLC-202.example: With TP=8, FP=2 and FN=4, precision is 0.8 and recall is 8/12, approximately 0.67.
MMLC-202.distinction: A high precision system may still miss many positive cases; choose measures based on consequences and class distribution.

MCSC-301.title: Research questions, claims and validity
MCSC-301.explanation: Align the research question, design, measurement, analysis and proposed claim. Internal validity concerns alternative explanations for an observed effect; external validity concerns whether results transfer to a defined context.
MCSC-301.example: A randomised comparison can reduce confounding under appropriate implementation; generalising from one class to all institutions requires additional evidence.
MCSC-301.distinction: Reliability concerns consistency of measurement; validity concerns whether the interpretation is supported.

MCSC-301.title: Search, citation and research ethics
MCSC-301.explanation: Document the databases, dates, queries, screening decisions and inclusion criteria used in a literature review. Cite sources accurately and disclose reuse; a similarity score requires human interpretation.
MCSC-301.example: A search log can record a database, the exact Boolean query, date, filters and the reason each full-text paper was excluded.
MCSC-301.distinction: A reference manager helps organise citations, but the researcher must verify bibliographic metadata and relevance.

MCSC-301.title: Sampling, power and uncertainty
MCSC-301.explanation: A sampling frame is the operational list from which participants are selected. Power depends on the effect of interest, variability, sample size, design and significance level.
MCSC-301.example: Increasing the sample size can reduce random uncertainty, but it will not eliminate systematic non-response bias.
MCSC-301.distinction: A statistically significant result does not establish a practically important effect or a sound research design.
